units.citation: (2017). Restauration de la productivité des sols tropicaux et méditerranéens. .
units.quote:
Par ailleurs, l’aménagement des fonds de ravines ralentit les crues lors des 
averses cycloniques et protège les plaines et villes des inondations brutales 
et de l’envasement des barrages. (English: Furthermore, treating the ravine floors slows floods during cyclonic storms and protects plains and towns from sudden floods and dam siltation.)

relationship.outcome_raw: treated ravine floors slow cyclonic-storm floods and protect downstream plains and towns

context.practice_as_described: Masonry and gabion check dams (seuils imperméables en gabions ou en maçonnerie de gros blocs avec mortier): eleven impermeable sills built across medium ravines of a 49 ha catchment where water was critical at the end of the dry season, sometimes with stilling basins or wells, to trap organic-rich sediment, infiltrate runoff and store water for irrigation and livestock; the trapped "fonds frais" are then cropped intensively (banana, malanga, yam, fruit trees, sugar cane, vegetables) with manure and residues (pp568-569). BASELINE: untreated ravines (implied).
context.note: Chapter 42 (Brochet, Clossy, Lilin, Roose), "Amenagements hydro-agricoles : capture des eaux et restauration de la productivite des sols - cas du bassin de Gros Morne en Haiti", PDF pp566-580. Development-project monitoring (SOS ESF); no research plots or soil analyses (p577); figures from annual monitoring reports (Brochet 2012). Assertion, no measurement; the conclusion (p579) hedges: "Il a probablement réduit aussi les crues". The authors add the main effect is to spread floods and reduce their shear and sediment transport. | Pete hold 2026-11-13: direction (less flooding) confirmed and the practice is check dams in ravine floors that capture runoff for irrigation (water harvesting, runoff catchment). The flood effect was not measured: the project had no research plots (p577) and the conclusion says only that it probably reduced floods (p579), so design is expert, not case_study.

units.question: Your hold, answered. You are right that the finding itself is good news and is coded that way: treating the ravine floors slows cyclone floods, which we record as less flooding. Nothing in it points to a conflict. The word 'conflicting' is about the headline rating, not this finding. Water harvesting's flood rating is set by a vote across its sub-practice groups (in-field works high, runoff-capture structures moderate, floodwater spreading moderate, terraces conflicting). The runoff-capture group rests on a handful of statements, and one of them says the opposite (Ritchie: bigger sand dams raise flood risk, see that item). Take away any one supporting statement and the opposite one weighs more than a third, so that group flips to conflicting and the vote moves. The rating is fragile, not the finding. Two honest caveats: the practice is check dams built across ravines to capture runoff and sediment for irrigation, which is water harvesting (runoff capture), so it belongs here; but the flood effect was never measured. The project had no research plots, and the conclusion says only that it 'probably' reduced floods. It is already marked as the authors' opinion; I have also corrected the study type from 'case study' to 'expert statement' so it carries the lower weight it should. Recommended: approve the corrected finding.

units.question: Your hold, answered. The review does not say which. The sentence comes from a modelling section and compares two ways of building sand dams: a few large dams against many smaller ones. Large dams store more water but carry more risk of flooding, erosion and seepage; many smaller dams carry less. It is second-hand, from a master's thesis model (Jansen 2007, Kenya) that we do not hold, and there is no word on whether the flooding is from failure, from overtopping, or every year. So it is not evidence that sand dams cause more flooding than having no dam. It is a design trade-off between dam sizes. Yet in the flood rating it sits as the one result saying water harvesting makes floods worse, and it is a main reason the runoff-capture group is so easily tipped into 'conflicting'. I recommend dropping it from the flood rating. On your modelling question: modelled results count with a weight like any study, but when a row's strength rests only on models, with no measured result behind it, the class is capped at moderate. This unit is both modelled and second-hand, and its comparison is the wrong one anyway. Recommended: reject.

units.question: Your hold, answered. Soil nitrogen is not something we invented. It is one of the two main outcomes of this meta-analysis, which pools 88 studies on soil carbon and soil nitrogen where cropland or bare land was returned to forest or grassland. Its headline result is that forest restoration gave no significant change in soil nitrogen (+3.04%, already a separate unit). This unit and its twin are subgroups of that same pool: the hot-climate studies (-16.84%) and the wet-climate studies (-19.85%), which overlap with each other and with the overall result. Counting the overall result and two slices of it as three findings breaks our 'one dataset, one finding' rule, and here the two slices outvote the paper's own headline. They are what pull the production-gap score to 'conflicting'. Recommend dropping both slices and keeping the overall result. Your wider point also stands: soil nitrogen reaches the production-gap score only through an indirect link (soil fertility as a component of yield), measured on land that has been taken out of cropping. Whether that link should exist for forest restoration is question 3. Recommended: reject.

units.question: Your hold, answered. SLM means 'sustainable land management'. WOCAT is a database of SLM technologies, and its sheets compare conditions 'before SLM' and 'after SLM', meaning before and after the technology was put in place. Here fire risk went from high to low, and we coded it as less fire, which is the right direction. Your objection is the right one, though. The person documenting it puts the fall in bush-fire risk down to the enclosure together with fire breaks and village bylaws, which are fire management, not forest regrowth. And the technology is not forest restoration. It fences off semi-natural grassland by a river, replants the boundary with Ficus trees, reseeds pasture legumes and grasses, adds fertiliser, and harvests the regrowth as cut-and-carry fodder and mulch. WOCAT files it as 'area closure' under silvo-pastoral land use. Our 'passive regeneration' group means forest coming back on its own with no planting. Recommend dropping it from forest restoration (wrong practice). If you would rather keep enclosures in forest restoration, it should at least be marked as a bundle with fire breaks and bylaws, so that it counts at a reduced share. Recommended: reject.

units.question: Your hold, answered. What we did: in a station trial in northern Burkina Faso, stone bunds raised millet grain by 15 to 50% in most years. But in the driest year (1985, 239 mm of rain) the yield with bunds was the same as without (136 against 137 kg/ha, Table 37). We recorded exactly that: no gain in a severe drought year. units.question: Your hold, answered. WOCAT asks the compiler to rate how the technology copes with each extreme on a five-step scale: not well at all, not well, moderately, well, very well. WOCAT does not say what each step means in damage. We chose a straight-line reading: very well = no damage, well = low, moderately = moderate, not well = high, not well at all = very high. So 'copes well' is read as the second-best step: it mostly withstands the event, with some sensitivity left, because 'very well' sits above it. That is a convention we chose, not WOCAT's. It is defensible as an ordinal reading, but it is a rule choice for you. Two other caveats. The question is ambiguous, and compilers may read it as 'how well does it help farmers cope' (this sheet lists 'fights floods, buffer role' as a strength). And it is one compiler's opinion, which already gets half weight. The 'low' damage rating is what 'copes well' implies; the alternative is to treat well and very well both as 'no meaningful damage'. See rule question 3. Needs your method decision (decision sheet, round 8); approve or hold here.

units.question: Your hold, answered. Agreed in principle, and this record is already the 'extreme wind makes it worse' half: it is tagged extreme (Category 4, 'when winds are so strong') and coded as shade trees adding damage. The catch is that this paper studied only one Category 4 hurricane. The benefit under ordinary winds appears only as the authors' expectation ('shade trees are likely to give some windbreak protection'), not something they measured. So we cannot add a measured 'helps in moderate wind' record from this source. For that we need windbreak or shade studies under ordinary storms. At extreme severity the paper's own result is mixed: some shaded patches were less damaged, toppled trees crushed coffee, and canopy cover did not predict damage. 'Conflicting' is an honest rating for extreme storms. What is missing is that the rating should say it applies to extreme storms only; see rule question 7. No change to the record. Recommended: approve (the finding stands).
